Rust owns the built-in client rows (adds host-agent-provider) and the new tables' rows (oauth-issuance); the sqliteRows full-content shape-parity check (M5) is as out of scope here as the existing D8.authz-row-counts decision already made for rowCounts.
Owner-approved reject-without-audit-writes: Go audits schema-invalid calls; Rust writes no rejected-call invocation record. The Rust contract fingerprints every database row.

Owner-approved refuse-before-operation-record: Go persists an operation row for a task-aware call before DispatchTool resolves its binding (internal/hostmcp/server.go:1644-1652), so a call refused at admission leaves a row and breaks X2; Rust records nothing durable for it. The wire task and its typed error are unchanged. The Rust contract fingerprints every database row.
The approved refusal contract omits precisely the refused task handle operation row in Rust. X2 independently requires Rust tables to be empty; no admitted row is exempted.

Rust's redact_for_storage (redact-unmarked-projections) replaces every unmarked/open-schema leaf under a durable row's structured content with the literal "[redacted]", recursively, regardless of field name or depth -- get_host_info's capacity/system/rootDiskQuota, get_vm_info's state, and similar open diagnostic objects across other capabilities' structured observations. Go's pinned reference persists the real value at the same positions; this is the declared, unchanged baseline, not a parity gap. dropValueDeep removes any such redacted leaf from both sides, converging them before comparison.

After workers drain, the single refused Go task has a cancelled operation snapshot. D12 requires Rust to omit that refused operation and its snapshot. Independent expectations require precisely cancelled on Go and no snapshot on Rust; late completed/failed snapshots fail before this projection is removed.

A provider callback into configure_network creates a delegated child task whose binding is refused (no such container). Go persists that refused task's operation row before resolving the binding (internal/hostmcp/server.go:1644-1652); Rust records nothing durable for it under owner decision D12. The scenario isolates exactly that row into its own query; the M7 verifier independently requires one working Go row and no Rust row, and every other operations row is still compared.

A provider callback creates a delegated configure_network child that the provider never acknowledges before the host shuts down. Go persists that never-started child's operation row at creation (internal/hostmcp/server.go:1642-1647) and restores it cancelled after a restart; under owner decision D18 (extending D12) Rust keeps nothing durable for it, so its rows are absent and its handle is unknown after the restart. The scenario isolates exactly the child's rows and its restored handle; per-side expectations pin Go's working then unknown row and cancelled handle and Rust's empty rows and task-not-found error, and every other step is compared.

Provider Alpha owns a capability family, provider Rival's install competes for it with an input schema the registry rejects, and provider Other then publishes a different family. The pinned Go displaces Alpha's registry entry before validating Rival (internal/hostmcp/server.go registerProviderServicesForGeneration), so Alpha's still-listed tool is refused as unregistered after the rejection and Other's publication drops it from tools/list. Under owner decision D16 Rust commits family displacement only with a valid candidate, so Alpha stays registered, listed and callable. The scenario isolates exactly Alpha's call after the rejection, the listing and Alpha's call after Other's publication, and Alpha's invocation audit rows; per-side expectations pin both sides and every other step, including Rival's rejection and Other's activation, is compared.

In the D16.rejected-candidate-keeps-owner scenario, the install response for provider Other reports the catalog revision current when Other's install began. The pinned Go registry had already lost Alpha's operation to Rival's rejected publication, so Go's revision describes a catalog without Alpha; Rust's describes one with Alpha, as the published tools/list on both sides did at that point. Only this one field of this one step is dropped; Alpha's presence is pinned per side by the scenario's expectations.

In the D16.rejected-candidate-keeps-owner scenario, the recipe run for provider Other reports the catalog revision current when Other's install began. The pinned Go registry had already lost Alpha's operation to Rival's rejected publication, so Go's revision describes a catalog without Alpha; Rust's describes one with Alpha, as the published tools/list on both sides did at that point. Only this one field of this one step is dropped; Alpha's presence is pinned per side by the scenario's expectations.

Database companion of D16.rejected-candidate-keeps-owner and D16.rollback-restores-owner, applied by the M5 shape check only to those scenarios. Alpha's calls after Rival's failed publication fail before any audit in Go and succeed in Rust, and in the rejected-candidate scenario the invocation Other's install plan records carries the catalog revision of a registry that has lost Alpha in Go. Invocation rows are keyed by random ids, so the table is dropped from the database comparison; each scenario's wire state step still compares every non-Alpha invocation's operation, generation, status and authorization, and alphaInvocations pins each side.

Database companion of D16.rejected-candidate-keeps-owner and D16.rollback-restores-owner: the invocation row count differs by Alpha's calls that Go no longer serves after Rival's failed publication and Rust serves.
Database companion of D16.other-run-catalog-revision: the catalog revision durable on Other's install plan run, which in Go counts a registry without Alpha. Only this field of this run is dropped.

Database companion of D16.rejected-candidate-keeps-owner: Other's generation records the catalog revision after its publication, which in Go no longer includes Alpha. Only this field of this generation is dropped.

Database companion of D18.unacknowledged-callback-child, applied by the M5 shape check only to that scenario: Go persists the never-acknowledged delegated child's operation row, Rust keeps nothing durable for it. Only the row keyed by the child's captured handle is dropped; the scenario's childRow and childRowRestored expectations pin each side.
Database companion of D18.unacknowledged-callback-child: the operations row count differs by exactly the child row Go persists.

Provider Alpha owns a capability family and provider Rival's install publishes a valid operation in it, which displaces Alpha, but Rival's service depends on a family nothing provides, so mounting fails and activation rolls back. The pinned Go rollback restores only Rival's own predecessor, so Alpha's operation is gone from tools/list and its call is an unknown tool. Under owner decision D16 Rust's rollback restores every family owner the activation displaced, so Alpha is listed and callable. The scenario isolates exactly the listing and Alpha's call after the rollback and Alpha's invocation audit rows; per-side expectations pin both sides and every other step, including Rival's rollback error, is compared.

Owner decision D20: when a compressed zstd block is corrupt, Go reports klauspost/compress's internal decoder message and Rust reports its own decoder's. Only the text after the 'extract host archive: ' prefix is dropped, and only in host-domain.archives.corrupt-blocks; whether the call fails, the prefix, the extracted tree and every other step are compared. Per-side expectations pin each side's exact text.

Owner decision D19 (openspec/changes/neutral-host-tool-names): Rust publishes provider-neutral names for the eight mapped host tools, keeps each Go name as a hidden alias, renames install_incus_stack.incusPackage to packageName, and therefore publishes different catalog revisions. Applied to the Rust side only, the rule rewrites each neutral name (whole words) to its Go name, the field inside that tool's input schema, and each Rust catalog revision pinned in parity-manifest.json to its Go pair, then restores the sorted order of any list the rename reordered. Every other difference, and every unpinned revision, remains a diff.
